blocks.text: Autumn begins in Columbus Indiana – with pleasant temperatures, rain, the fall colors ranging from the sacred yellows to the golden browns and the flaming reds, mums and marigolds in full bloom and the smell of pumpkin spice in every home. The spiritual aura of being one with nature and enjoying the bounty of harvest is in the air. It’s time to celebrate in most agricultural families and that’s how I think, Festivals, first came into being. They are our way of thanking the powers that be for getting all the stars aligned and contributing to our success this year and to pray for a better next year.

Being from India but living in the Mid West USA, I have had the privilege and joy of celebrating both Indian and American autumn festivals. The one festival I’d like to concentrate on for this post is NAVARATHRI – an Indian festival which literally means “Nine Nights”. The dates for this festival are determined according to the lunar Hindu calendar. Raj (my husband) started celebrating this festival in our home 8 years ago and we have loved continuing this tradition every year.

I would like to remind readers that India is vastly diverse in the way we celebrate festivals. The following is the way, I celebrated Navarathri as a kid growing up in the southern state of Tamil Nadu.

According to Wikipedia, the beginning of autumn is an important junction of climatic and solar influence and is taken as an opportunity for the worship of the Divine Mother – who like all mothers is a perfect harmony of Creation, Preservation and Destruction. God is worshipped in the form of a Mother, who loves all her children unconditionally.

blocks.name: Parvati
blocks.text: Goddess Parvati or Shakti (Goddess of Power) is worshipped on the first 3 days and her blessings are invoked to destroy all bad vibes and impurities.

blocks.name: Lakshmi
blocks.text: Goddess Lakshmi (Goddess of Wealth) is worshipped on the second 3 days to provide everyone with spiritual and literal wealth (to keep everyone happy, healthy and wealthy).

blocks.name: Saraswati
blocks.text: Goddess Saraswati (Goddess of Wisdom) is worshipped on the last 3 days to obtain wisdom that will lead to eternal happiness and Moksha.

blocks.name: Saraswati Poojai · Ayudha Poojai
blocks.text: The ninth day is celebrated as Saraswati Poojai and Ayudha Poojai (Worship of Tools) during which all tools, vehicles, pens, pencils, calculators and books are ceremoniously cleaned and worshipped so that their powers get replenished and they continue to serve us well for the next year. School going children use this as an opportunity to put all their books in poojai so that they get one day of all-out fun (no studying).

blocks.name: Vijayadasami
blocks.text: The grand culmination of festivities is on the 10th day – Vijayadasami. This day is considered auspicious for new beginnings. All the books and tools worshipped the previous day are taken out for a spin. It is customary to read a few lines from every book kept in poojai. The kids who had all-out fun the previous day have to buckle down and read today with their parents. In early times, all tiny tots, ready for education, started school on this day. Also, toddlers on their dad’s lap learnt to write their native alphabets in rice on this day.

The day before Navarathri is a new moon and is known as the Mahalaya Amavasai. An odd number of steps (3, 5, 7, 9 or 11) is set up in a spacious area in the home and a white fabric is used to cover the steps to give a good canvas for the vibrantly colored dolls which will go on display. All dolls that have been collected over the years in the family are taken out and arranged on these steps. The tradition is to have clay and wooden dolls of Gods and Goddesses on the top steps. Human dolls follow depicting various scenes like a wedding, a musical concert, people celebrating festivals et cetera. A wooden couple (man and woman) is mandatory in Golu. This is so important that a wooden couple is presented to a newly married daughter by her mother to continue the Golu tradition at her in-law’s place. The last few steps are dedicated to animals, birds, plants and other non-living things like pots, pans, pulses, rice etc. Nowadays, the dolls have grown more modern… they even depict people playing cricket or dancing to music. Some ladies go gung-ho and grow grass for a park where kids and dogs are depicted playing and having fun. I have even seen entire cities being created and connected by train-sets which choo their way around the lit up track.

The first day of Navarathri, a pot filled with water and rice is placed in the middle step with a coconut and mango leaves on top of it. This is called the Kalasam. After this pot is placed on the step, the dolls can no longer be moved till the end of Golu. Two beautiful lit lamps are placed on either side of the steps to draw attention to the dolls.

Usually, Moms make a new salty and a sweet prasadam are made as offerings to God every day during this festival. The sweet prasadam is usually oozing with ghee and I believe this is to make people feel warm in the coming cold months of the year. The salty prasadam is a perfect complement to the sweet and is made of boiled/fried pulses, coconut and red chillies. Always brings water to my mouth!

Friends and relatives are invited to homes and poojai is performed in front of the Golu dolls. Girls and women are the special guests and they sing hymns about the Divine Mother and how she helps everyone overcome adversity and showers blessings. Stories are told about the mythology behind each doll. I hypothesize that this ritual began as a secret way for elders to pass on the wisdom of ages and age old inspiring tales to the younger generation and as an opportunity for Indian women (who were eternally bound to upkeep of their homes and families) to get together and bond. Children are usually in their best traditional attire and are taught how to be gracious hosts and guests. Kumkumam, prasadam and a gift bag with goodies for women and girls is given at each home.

On the evening of Vijayadasami, one doll from the Golu is symbolically put to sleep and the Kalasam is moved a bit towards North to mark the end of Golu. Prayers are offered to thank God for the successful completion of Golu with the hope of a successful one the next year. Then the Golu is dismantled and packed up for the next year.
It is so fresh in my mind that I can still smell the prasadam and the ghee and see the vibrantly colored dolls arranged so methodically on the steps.

Being a true red-blooded Tamilian, I miss home very dearly during this festival and so would like to dedicate this post to all moms who toil hard in the kitchen and pooja room to make our childhood so memorable. It is so fresh in my mind that I can still smell the prasadam and the ghee and see the vibrantly colored dolls arranged so methodically on the steps.

glossary.poojai: Poojai: worship of God during which some offering is made
glossary.moksha: Moksha: self realization leading to the end of all the suffering involved in the cycle of repeated death and rebirth.
